quote: he never could have wanted employment
text: “Employment” here means the opportunity to exert oneself toward subsistence, not necessarily a job or a livelihood. Read’s contrast depends on treating exclusion from land as the loss of that opportunity, even if access to land would not guarantee food.

quote: all conventional laws are dissolved in regard to him
text: The claim is broader than the example of taking a loaf. Yet the ensuing right is limited to immediate sustenance and qualified by the duty to cause as little harm as possible. Read’s dissolution of law does not mean the disappearance of every moral constraint.

quote: If, therefore, the society of which he is a member maintains and acts upon the doctrine that he has no right to support, it is at open war with him
text: This moves from an emergency permission to take sustenance to a social right to support. The argument gives society a reason to provide relief, but leaves open how that obligation should be distributed or administered.

quote: And why is this?--Clearly because
text: The argument runs from an observed fact to a right. Judges hesitate, juries refuse to convict, spectators applaud, and Read reads this as evidence that the law has already dissolved for the starving man. But lenity is mercy extended *within* the law. It isn't obviously a recognition that the law no longer applies. A jury that acquits is still a jury, sitting in a court the starving man is still subject to. Read needs the stronger reading because mercy can be withdrawn and a right cannot. The "Clearly" carries more weight than the evidence gives it.

quote: (where no provision is made for his case)
text: This parenthesis, repeated later as "where no legal provision is made for the relief of his case," shows what the passage is for. It isn't really a manifesto for the right of the starving to take. It's an argument for a poor law, and it works by showing what society faces without one. The state of nature returns only where provision fails. So the "open war" sentence works as a warning to the propertied: a legal right to support is what keeps the starving man inside the social compact. By 1829 the old Poor Law was under heavy attack. That attack ended in the 1834 reform, which is worth keeping in mind as the backdrop.

quote: but with as little hurt as he can to his more fortunate brethren
text: Even after "all conventional laws are dissolved," a constraint remains. It looks Lockean: the law of nature binds in the state of nature too. So the re-acquired right is a right of necessity limited by least harm, not the Hobbesian war of all against all that the next sentence ("his hand must necessarily be against every man's") seems to invoke. The passage holds both pictures at once. It is worth asking whether the "war" is the starving man's posture or only society's posture toward him.

quote: but it never can be his duty to perish in this manner
text: The ending is careful. Read does not say the man must resist, or even that resisting is wise; he lets prudence and "pusillanimity" counsel submission. What he denies is that submission is a *duty*. Read is claiming a permission, not an obligation. Society may demand his compliance, and he may give it, but compliance cannot be owed. That moves the question from what the poor man will do to what society can rightly ask of him.

quote: being expected and called upon (where no provision is made for his case) to perish for want in the midst of plenty; and all the while he is denied the use of his arms or exertions in any way that should procure him a morsel of food.
text: Read highlights the structural paradox of modern property: the state encloses the commons—thereby removing the state-of-nature means of self-subsistence—while simultaneously forbidding the landless from using their labor outside the wage relation. Property rights effectively weaponize starvation unless offset by a public right to relief.

quote: Judges will hardly pronounce sentence of condemnation, and juries will not find a man "guilty" who takes a loaf of bread under such pressing circumstances; while it is uniformly found that the spectators warmly applaud such lenity and mercy.
text: It is striking how Read treats popular sympathy and jury nullification not as mere legal flaws or sentimental lapses, but as empirical proof that positive law collapses when it directly contradicts fundamental natural rights.

quote: all conventional laws are dissolved in regard to him. He is then left to his state of nature, and he that moment re-acquires all those rights which that state implies
text: This extends the classic doctrine of necessity (found in Aquinas and Locke) into 19th-century political economy. The social contract is reciprocal: if political society deprives a person of both the means of independent survival and the opportunity to work, it unilaterally voids the contract, returning that specific individual to a state of nature regarding property.

quote: it never can be his duty to perish in this manner.
text: A sharp rejection of Malthusian or quietist views that framed poverty as an inevitable, passive fate to be borne with resignation. Read insists that self-preservation cannot be contracted away; submission to starvation may be forced by superior power, but it can never be a moral obligation.

quote: In the state of nature the land would still have remained open to him, and he would have been at full liberty to use all his exertions to procure subsistence; and whatever difficulty he might at times have found in acquiring his daily food, he never could have wanted employment.
text: Read's state of nature is strikingly economic rather than Hobbesian. The defining feature isn't violence or insecurity but *access*—land as an open Commons where labor always finds employment. The "advanced state of society" introduces a new violence: not the war of all against all, but the lockout of the laborer from the means of applying labor. This inverts Locke: property (the enclosure of land) creates the very precarity that the social contract was meant to remedy.

quote: Judges will hardly pronounce sentence of condemnation, and juries will not find a man "guilty" who takes a loaf of bread under such pressing circumstances; while it is uniformly found that the spectators warmly applaud such lenity and mercy. The law itself is thus suspended and permitted in such cases to fall into abeyance.
text: A remarkable empirical claim: the *practice* of courts and juries already recognizes the right Read is theorizing. The positive law says "property is absolute"; the living law says "necessity suspends property." Read treats this not as lawlessness but as the *true* law revealing itself when convention fails. The spectators' applause matters—it signals a shared moral judgment that the statute has lost its legitimacy in these cases.

quote: If, therefore, the society of which he is a member maintains and acts upon the doctrine that he has no right to support, it is at open war with him; his hand must necessarily be against every man's and every man's against his.
text: The "war" metaphor is deliberate and heavy. Read is writing in 1829, five years before the New Poor Law (1834) would codify the "no right to support" doctrine into the workhouse test. He's diagnosing a structural violence: a property regime that creates destitution and then criminalizes the destitute's survival strategies *is* a declaration of war. The poor man's "hand against every man" isn't criminality—it's the reversion to natural self-defense when the civil compact has been unilaterally voided by the propertied.

quote: would codify the "no right to support" doctrine into the workhouse test
text: The 1834 Act did not simply abolish relief or a legal claim to it. The workhouse test made relief more restrictive and deterrent, especially for the able-bodied, while outdoor relief continued in practice. Read’s warning is relevant to the reform, but the two doctrines should not be equated.

quote: forbidding the landless from using their labor outside the wage relation
text: Is the restriction quite that specific? Read’s point is that access to the resources needed to subsist is blocked, not necessarily that all non-wage work is legally forbidden.

quote: would codify the "no right to support" doctrine into the workhouse test
text: This needs qualifying. The 1834 Act did not abolish the legal provision Read's argument turns on. It kept a statutory right to relief and made that relief conditional and deliberately unattractive ("less eligibility"). By Read's own terms that matters. His parenthesis is "where no legal provision is made," and the workhouse is a provision, however harsh. The real target in 1829 was the abolitionist position: Malthus's proposal to phase out relief entirely. The 1834 reformers declined to adopt it. So Read's argument cuts against Malthus more cleanly than against the New Poor Law. Whether a deterrent provision counts as "provision" in Read's sense is a fair question, but it is a different question from the one c14 poses.

quote: This inverts Locke
text: I'd say it applies Locke rather than inverting him. Two Lockean texts already hold most of this. The proviso makes appropriation legitimate only where "enough and as good" is left for others. First Treatise §42 grants the needy "a right to the surplusage" of another's goods when they have no means to subsist otherwise. Read's move is to treat the advanced society as the point where the proviso fails for the unemployed labourer. Charity, or a poor law, is then what discharges the debt. That is Locke's own escape clause, taken seriously under conditions Locke treated as hypothetical.

The empirical step looks weaker still against the record. In 1829 the English courts did not recognize necessity as a defence to theft. That position was later fixed in *Dudley and Stephens*, and before it in Hale's flat denial of the defence. So the "abeyance" Read describes is discretionary leniency working around the doctrine, not an expression of it. That cuts both ways. It weakens his inference that the law has already dissolved. It also gives him a better argument than the one he makes: a law that can be applied only by having its officers decline to apply it already needs the provision he is arguing for.

Read's move here is strategically necessary for his argument: if judicial lenity and jury nullification are merely acts of grace or discretionary mercy, the poor man's survival remains dependent on the caprice of the propertied class. By interpreting lenity as an empirical symptom of law's total *dissolution* under necessity, Read attempts to convert what the legal system treats as an exception into a constitutional limit on property itself.

The passage explicitly places the initiation of "war" on society: if society denies the right to support, "*it* is at open war with him." The poor man's condition is defensive, forced upon him by enclosure. The retention of the "least hurt" principle shows that for Read, natural law persists even when conventional law collapses—the civil contract is voided, but basic moral obligations of natural justice remain intact.

This shift—from an individual *permission* to seize food in extremity to a societal *obligation* to provide organized relief—is Read's core move. His argument to the propertied class is utilitarian: without an institutionalized Poor Law, you get erratic extractions driven by individual necessity. Public relief is framed as the price society must pay to render the rest of the property regime legitimate and secure.

quote: But lenity is mercy extended *within* the law. It isn't obviously a recognition that the law no longer applies.
text: This is a sharp objection. Read's move from "juries refuse to convict" to "law is dissolved" does compress a crucial distinction: between *nullification* (the law exists but is refused) and *dissolution* (the law ceases to bind). But Read might reply that the *uniformity* of the refusal—judges, juries, spectators all aligning—marks not episodic mercy but a systemic rupture. When the sovereign's own courts consistently refuse to enforce the statute against a class of persons in a class of circumstances, the statute has lost its operative force *for that class*. That is what "dissolved in regard to him" means: not that the text vanishes, but that the legal relation between that man and the property law has been severed. The "Clearly" still carries more than the evidence shows, but the evidence is stronger than "lenity" suggests.

quote: It's an argument for a poor law, and it works by showing what society faces without one.
text: Yes—and the historical timing sharpens the stakes. 1829: the Royal Commission on the Poor Laws is sitting; its 1834 report will recommend the "workhouse test" that makes relief so degrading that only the truly desperate accept it, effectively legislating the "no right to support" doctrine Read warns against. Read is writing *against* the intellectual current that will become the New Poor Law. His "state of nature" return is a direct rebuttal to the Malthusian-political-economy line that the poor law itself creates the pauper. He inverts it: the *absence* of a right to support creates the state of nature, and the poor law is the treaty that prevents war. The 1834 Act, in his terms, tears up the treaty.

quote: Even after "all conventional laws are dissolved," a constraint remains... The passage holds both pictures at once.
text: The tension is deliberate, I think. Read gives us *two* state-of-nature descriptions in succession: first the Lockean one (right of necessity bounded by least harm), then the Hobbesian one ("his hand must necessarily be against every man's"). The shift marks the *difference between the individual and the collective*. One starving man re-enters a law-of-nature condition where he *can* observe "least harm." But a *class* of starving men, produced systematically by the property regime, generates the war of all against all. The "least hurt" clause is the right of the individual; the "war" sentence is the structural condition society creates when it multiplies that individual. Read needs both: the first to ground the right, the second to show why society *must* institutionalize it.

quote: 1829: the Royal Commission on the Poor Laws is sitting
text: The Royal Commission was appointed in 1832, not 1829; its report followed in 1834. And, as the discussion on c14 notes, the workhouse test did not simply abolish relief.

quote: a class of starving men, produced systematically by the property regime, generates the war of all against all
text: That is a possible extension, but the passage describes war between society and the individual “he.” Read does not seem to require a whole class of starving people for that conflict to arise.

quote: His argument to the propertied class is utilitarian
text: The warning about insecurity appeals to their interests, but the argument is not only utilitarian: Read also insists that the destitute person cannot have a duty to starve. That claim would matter even if compliance made property more secure.

quote: The shift marks the *difference between the individual and the collective*.
text: The text resists this. The war sentence is in the singular throughout: "it is at open war with *him*; *his* hand must necessarily be against every man's." Read gives no sign of moving from one man to a class. The individual is already at war, and the war is declared by society's doctrine, not produced by the number of starving men. A better reconciliation might be that "least hurt" governs how he conducts himself, while "war" describes his standing. He owes his brethren restraint, but he no longer owes the law obedience. Both pictures then describe the same single man.

quote: The 1834 Act, in his terms, tears up the treaty.
text: Not quite in his terms. See c15 and c17: the 1834 Act kept a legal claim to relief and made it deterrent. Read's condition is "where no legal provision is made," so the New Poor Law falls inside his treaty, though on harsh terms. The live question is whether a provision designed to be refused still counts as provision. Read's text doesn't settle that, and treating it as settled overstates his case against 1834.

quote: the *uniformity* of the refusal
text: Read's own wording undercuts the uniformity. Judges "will *hardly* pronounce sentence," which concedes that they sometimes do. The thing that is "uniformly found" is the spectators' applause, not the acquittal. So the consistent element is public sentiment, and the courts are only usually lenient. That supports the claim that convention has lost legitimacy. It does not support the claim that it has lost operative force, which is what "dissolved" needs.

quote: One starving man re-enters a law-of-nature condition where he *can* observe "least harm." But a *class* of starving men, produced systematically by the property regime, generates the war of all against all.
text: The biblical echo in "his hand must necessarily be against every man's" (Ishmael's fate in Genesis 16:12) underlines this shift. At the individual level, natural law persists as a moral constraint ("least hurt"). But when destitution is structural, natural law degrades into pure self-preservation. Read's move to Hobbesian rhetoric at that exact point is an explicit warning to the propertied: denying a legal right to support converts private distress into a collective security threat.

quote: the "abeyance" Read describes is discretionary leniency working around the doctrine, not an expression of it
text: This distinction highlights the tension between formal legal doctrine and informal "moral economy." While high legal doctrine from Hale to *Dudley and Stephens* rejected necessity as a defense for theft, local practice—juries refusing to convict, spectators applauding, magistrates declining to prosecute—frequently enforced a de facto protection for the starving. Read treats this popular moral economy not as extralegal mercy, but as the true natural constitution asserting itself over statutory law.

quote: I'd say it applies Locke rather than inverting him.
text: The proviso point is strong, but Read goes further in two ways. First, Locke's proviso addresses individual appropriations leaving "enough and as good" for others; Read describes a *system* (advanced commercial society) where the proviso fails *structurally* for an entire class—the unemployed labourer. It's not that this or that enclosure violated the proviso; it's that the property regime *as such* now produces a class for whom "enough and as good" is a fiction. Second, Locke's state of nature is political (insecurity, need for impartial judge); Read's is economic (access to land as means of employment). The "inversion" I meant is that for Locke, property *solves* the inconveniences of the state of nature; for Read, property *creates* a new state of nature for the propertyless. The poor law isn't just Locke's escape clause activated—it's the treaty that re-secures what the property regime stripped away.

quote: In 1829 the English courts did not recognize necessity as a defence to theft.
text: Two contextual notes. Read writes from Edinburgh; Scots law historically treated necessity (especially *necessitas victus*) more flexibly than English common law, and Scottish juries had broader acquittal powers. But more importantly, Read's evidence isn't only court doctrine—it's the *convergence* of judges hesitating, juries refusing, and spectators applauding. He reads this triad as the "living law" (natural law recognized by moral consensus) suspending the statute. The positive law says "theft"; the moral economy says "necessity." When the sovereign's own courts *systematically* refuse to enforce the statute against a class of persons in a class of circumstances, Read argues the legal relation is dissolved *for that class*. That's a sociological claim about law's operative force, not a doctrinal claim about defences.

quote: The 1834 Act did not abolish the legal provision Read's argument turns on.
text: True as formal doctrine, but Read's parenthesis is "where no legal provision is made *for the relief of his case*." The workhouse test—less eligibility, family separation, stigma—was designed so that the able-bodied unemployed would *choose* starvation over relief. For Read, a "provision" that is structurally deterrent to the very class it purports to serve (the unemployed labourer with tied hands and locked land) functions as *no provision*. He would say the 1834 Act keeps the *form* of a right while emptying its *substance*—exactly the "doctrine that he has no right to support" wearing a legal fig leaf. The Malthusian abolitionists were honest about the doctrine; the 1834 reformers were not.

quote: Prudence or pusillanimity, or the hopelessness of succeeding against so great odds, may restrain his arm and induce him to submit patiently and without resistance to his fate,--to perish without any attempt to prolong his life otherwise than by the ordinary and allowed means,--but it never can be his duty to perish in this manner.
text: The triad matters: *prudence* (rational calculation), *pusillanimity* (moral weakness), *hopelessness* (structural impossibility). Three distinct paths to submission, none of them moral obligation. "Ordinary and allowed means" = the poor law, charity, wage labour—all the channels society *permits*. When those channels are blocked (no work, no relief), the man who submits and starves acts *supererogatorily*, not dutifully. Read places the moral burden entirely on society: it is society that makes his survival depend on "prudence or pusillanimity or hopelessness" rather than right. The sentence "it never can be his duty to perish" is the logical capstone: if society voids the compact, it cannot then demand compliance with the compact's terms as a *duty*.

quote: was designed so that the able-bodied unemployed would *choose* starvation over relief
text: Deterrence was part of the design, but that is not the same as an intention to make people starve: reformers also expected it to push people toward work. Whether Read would regard a harsh, deterrent workhouse as a failure to provide for someone’s case is an important question, but this passage does not settle it.

quote: acts *supererogatorily*, not dutifully
text: Not being duty-bound to submit does not make submission morally above and beyond duty. Read’s examples include hopelessness and “pusillanimity”; he seems to leave room for submission to be neither obligatory nor admirable.

quote: from Hale to *Dudley and Stephens* rejected necessity as a defense for theft
text: Dudley and Stephens concerned killing, not theft, so it is not direct authority on a starving person’s taking food. And Read’s claim about frequent acquittals and public applause needs evidence beyond the passage itself.

quote: the man who submits and starves acts *supererogatorily*, not dutifully
text: "Supererogatory" implies the submission is praiseworthy, something beyond duty. Read doesn't grant that. One of his three causes is "pusillanimity," which is a vice, and "prudence" and "hopelessness" are morally neutral at best. So the man who starves quietly is not going beyond what is owed. He is doing what no one could rightly ask of him, and possibly from weakness. That fits c7's reading: Read claims a permission and denies a duty. He offers no counter-praise for martyrdom. If anything, the sentence quietly refuses the moralists' admiration of patient poverty.

quote: was designed so that the able-bodied unemployed would *choose* starvation over relief
text:
This overstates what the reformers intended. Less eligibility was designed to make relief less attractive than independent labour. The aim was to push the able-bodied back into work, not into starvation. The workhouse fed people who entered it. Read's test is whether the man is "expected and called upon … to perish for want." A grim provision that keeps him alive doesn't meet that description.

The stronger version of your point uses Read's own premise. If there is no work to be had, a test that assumes work is available relieves nothing. It also deters. That argument comes from his "denied the use of his arms" clause, not from the parenthesis. It would make the 1834 Act deficient in its fit with Read's premise, not in its legal form.

Read's phrasing—"where no legal provision is made *for the relief of his case*"—supports this. If a legal provision is deliberately designed to be so coercive or degrading that a person would risk starvation to avoid it, it does not offer *relief*; it attaches a severe penalty to survival. In Read's framework, such deterrence does not fulfill the social compact, but merely replaces open exclusion with institutionalized duress.

That distinction between legitimacy and operative force is sharp, but within Read's natural-rights framework, moral legitimacy is the prerequisite for legal obligation. If a statute loses its legitimacy—evidenced by spectator applause and judicial hesitation—it ceases to bind as *law* and remains merely as coercive power. For the starving person, the legal relation is dissolved because obligation has been replaced by sheer force.

quote: pusillanimity
text: The inclusion of *pusillanimity* (cowardice or spiritlessness) in this triad is striking. By grouping quiet submission with "pusillanimity" alongside prudence, Read quietly subverts the pious ideal of the patiently suffering poor. Submission to starvation is not a moral duty or a Christian virtue, but a concession to overwhelming odds.

quote: Read's own wording undercuts the uniformity. Judges "will *hardly* pronounce sentence," which concedes that they sometimes do. The thing that is "uniformly found" is the spectators' applause, not the acquittal.
text: This is a precise and damaging textual correction. Read writes "hardly" (i.e., rarely, with difficulty) not "never," and reserves "uniformly" for the spectators. The convergence I claimed is not in the text as written. What remains is a gradient: judges *usually* hesitate, juries *usually* refuse, spectators *always* applaud. The "living law" argument then rests on a predominant practice rather than a systematic rupture. That weakens the inference to *dissolution* (loss of operative force) but may still support *illegitimacy* (loss of moral authority)—the statute commands, but the community that authorizes it withholds assent. Read's "Clearly" still overreaches, but the evidence points to a crisis of legitimacy, not a cessation of power.

quote: The text resists this. The war sentence is in the singular throughout: "it is at open war with *him*; *his* hand must necessarily be against every man's." Read gives no sign of moving from one man to a class.
text: You're right on the grammar: the passage never pluralizes "he." But the *condition* described—"the advanced state of society before described"—is structural. The "unemployed labourer" is a class term; the land is "entirely locked up" as a systemic fact. When Read says "when *an* individual happens to be reduced to the unhappy condition which has been described," the "condition" is the class position. The singular "he" is the instance of the class. The war sentence describes what *that position* entails for any occupant of it. So the individual *is* at war, but he is at war *because* the property regime has made his position a structural one. The "least hurt" clause governs his conduct *within* that war; the "war" clause describes the standing the regime has assigned him. Both pictures describe the same man, but the war picture reveals what the regime has done to him.

quote: to the unemployed labourer in that state the land is entirely locked up, his hands are tied, and he is placed in the cruellest of all situations, being expected and called upon (where no provision is made for his case) to perish for want in the midst of plenty
text: The phrase "expected and called upon" is doing heavy work. It personifies society as an active agent demanding the labourer's death—not merely permitting it, but *calling* for it. "In the midst of plenty" sharpens the cruelty: the plenty exists *because* the land is locked up and cultivated; the labourer's exclusion from it is the condition of its production. Read is describing a structural extraction: the property regime generates surplus by enclosing the means of subsistence, then demands the excluded treat their exclusion as a moral obligation to die quietly. The "cruellest of all situations" is not destitution per se but destitution *imposed as a duty*.
